questions.stem: Digestion involves both mechanical and chemical processes. Chewing food in the mouth is an example of mechanical digestion. Why does breaking food into smaller pieces help chemical digestion?

options.text: Smaller pieces dissolve faster in stomach acid
Smaller pieces have a larger total surface area for digestive enzymes to act on
Smaller pieces contain fewer nutrients
Chewing kills bacteria in the food

questions.explanation: Breaking food into smaller pieces by chewing (and later by churning in the stomach) increases the total surface area exposed to digestive enzymes. This allows more enzyme molecules to contact the food at the same time, speeding up the rate of chemical digestion. This is similar to how crushing a sugar cube makes it dissolve faster.

questions.stem: Bile is alkaline and is released into the small intestine. One of its roles is to neutralise the acidic chyme from the stomach. Why is this neutralisation important?

options.text: Intestinal enzymes need an alkaline environment (pH 7-8) to function at their optimum
Acid would dissolve the small intestine wall
Alkaline conditions stop all enzyme activity
Bile converts acid into water

questions.explanation: Stomach acid (pH 1-2) would denature the enzymes in the small intestine (such as pancreatic lipase, amylase, and trypsin), which have an optimum pH of around 7-8. Bile's alkaline nature neutralises the acid, creating the correct pH for intestinal enzymes to work effectively.

questions.stem: Large food molecules like proteins, starch, and fats must be digested into smaller molecules before they can be absorbed. Why can't the large molecules be absorbed directly?

options.text: Large molecules are toxic to blood cells
Large molecules are too big to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood
Large molecules would block the villi
Only small molecules contain useful energy

questions.explanation: Large biological molecules (polymers like proteins, starch, and fats) are too big to pass through the epithelial cells lining the small intestine. They must be broken down into their smaller, soluble subunits (amino acids, glucose, fatty acids, and glycerol) which are small enough to cross the intestinal wall into the bloodstream.

questions.stem: A patient takes an antacid tablet to relieve heartburn. The antacid neutralises excess stomach acid. What effect might this have on protein digestion in the stomach?

options.text: Protein digestion would increase because enzymes work better without acid
Protein digestion would decrease because pepsin needs acidic conditions (pH 2) to function
Protein digestion would not be affected
All protein would be instantly digested

questions.explanation: Pepsin, the protease enzyme in the stomach, has an optimum pH of about 2. Antacids raise the pH, moving it away from pepsin's optimum, which reduces its activity. This is why antacids can sometimes cause bloating or indigestion -- protein digestion in the stomach is temporarily impaired, though it continues in the small intestine with trypsin.

questions.stem: The pancreas produces enzymes including amylase, lipase, and trypsin. These are released into the duodenum. Why does the pancreas produce these enzymes rather than each intestinal cell making its own?

options.text: Intestinal cells cannot produce any enzymes
Centralised enzyme production by a specialised organ allows large quantities to be released when needed for efficient digestion
The pancreas is closer to the food than the intestinal cells
Pancreatic enzymes are different from all other enzymes

questions.explanation: The pancreas is a specialised gland that can produce and secrete large quantities of digestive enzymes efficiently. This ensures an adequate supply is released into the duodenum when food arrives from the stomach. While intestinal cells do produce some enzymes, the pancreas provides the bulk of digestive enzymes needed for effective digestion.
